name: Jade Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead water-treatment control software at a tech company, where I am among the strongest at tracing a sensor error. I never use AI tools and compare each dose change with an operator’s signed sheet. Imani repairs bicycles, our children are grown, and higher lead pay has helped us own a flat and save fourteen months of expenses; many software firms are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the water-treatment team that a small AI shortcut can tidy a log, but a chemical dose still needs the right measurement. I never use AI tools; I compare my control-code changes with the plant’s signed test sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead this software team at a tech company, where I am one of the strongest at tracing a bad sensor reading. Imani repairs bicycles, our children are grown, and higher lead pay has helped us own a flat and save fourteen months of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing the dose-control code with the plant operator each Wednesday. We would save 260 monthly while both incomes hold and repair the balcony railing rather than replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our jobs and bills. Clear water does not excuse an untraceable dose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you catch in a test sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One sensor said the tank was full after it had been drained for cleaning. I checked the signed operator sheet before changing the dose command.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why no AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need to trace every number to a sensor and a person. An answer I cannot reproduce does not belong in the plant log.

I want **operator review** on each dose change that reaches the treatment tank.
think: I have **fourteen months saved** from higher lead pay and Imani’s repair work.
I see **housing secure** with our paid-off flat and fourteen-month reserve.

**Save 260 monthly** while both incomes hold; repair balcony rail before replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking checking, planning and coding could reduce our control team, but the plant must name the person who signs a dose change. I would ask the staff association to demand written staffing and override rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own lead role could shrink if a single engineer watches several automated plants. Fourteen months saved gives us time, but Imani’s workshop income cannot replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the association meeting this month to request written funded lead hours and a named human override. I’d keep recording real sensor discrepancies with the operator; if my paid hours fall, I’d search local paid plant-software vacancies only if wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own wage and a rushed safety change. A fast graph cannot sign a water sample.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask how many paid reviewer hours remain and who can stop an automated dose. I would join the group request, not claim to bargain alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI control assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used one, and I would not start with a plant where people drink the result.

I want **named dose overrides** when automated systems suggest a chemical change.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** across automated plants.
I cannot replace **my developer wage** with Imani’s workshop income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write the dose code and interpret water tests more cheaply than our team. Robots doing physical sampling and bicycle repair may follow around 2031, after screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could end my lead developer role despite years of careful work. Fourteen months saved would give us search time, but Imani’s workshop cannot pay every household bill alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d postpone the planned bathroom renovation and ask for written notice of any lead cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local water-quality software openings only where vacancies exist and wages cover our bills; I would not take an unpaid plant placement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing my own wage. A signed water sheet is evidence, not a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you become a plant operator immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know the control code, not the full physical-sampling qualification. I would only apply where my current skills meet the paid job’s rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children fund the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own homes, and our savings are there so we can search for paid work ourselves.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach dose code first.
I expect **sampling robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **lead developer wage** could end.
I know **fourteen months saved** is search time, not income.
do: **Postpone bathroom renovation** and request written cut notice now.

S2.quote: A signed water sheet is evidence, not a salary.
fieldNote: She avoids claiming **plant-operator qualification** from software expertise.
A **paid local vacancy** and bill-covering wage are required despite strong savings and considerable control-code experience at the plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives workers time to demand clear responsibility for dose overrides before code changes. Robots collecting samples may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could spend these years showing which manual checks catch a bad sensor, though AGI may eventually catch them too. I do not want to buy a new profession when my current skill and a long reserve give me time to demand a funded role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the association’s quarterly meeting to request a funded human dose-review position and keep a dated log of operator-verified sensor errors while my job pays. We would save 240 monthly while both incomes hold; if my developer role ends after 2031, I’d apply for paid local water-safety software vacancies only if real openings and wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my lead role but less rushed than in the two-year case. A log of real errors is stronger than a promise of oversight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in the log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sensor value, the operator’s physical reading and the correction we made to the code. I would remove customer details before sharing it with the association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if management refuses a funded review post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid developer job while it exists and continue documenting errors. I would not count an unfunded position as another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 lets plants and workers make dose decisions traceable and staffing agreements written. Robots taking physical water samples may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may choose to stop paid work later, but I have not verified a retirement amount. Our flat and fourteen months saved make the next few years secure; no future plant post is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing dose code and join the association’s annual review of funded human override hours. We would save 250 monthly while both incomes hold and request a written retirement-income estimate; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local water-safety software vacancies only if openings and wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about work later but secure in the next few years. Water that looks clear still needs a recorded test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual review ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask for the number of paid override hours and the person authorised to stop a dose. I want those names and hours recorded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for the plant work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would search nearby plants and software firms. Imani’s repair shop and our flat are here, so I am not planning a move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could end before another paid water-safety opening exists. Written notice, funded human override work if management agrees, and a real bill-covering local vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a clear-looking tank proves our software is safe. I would rather keep a signed test than a confident story about clear water.

headlineQuote: I would rather keep a signed test than a confident story about clear water.
portrait: Jade is a **58-year-old software lead** with a master’s degree, higher pay and fourteen months saved.
She and Imani own **a flat** while their grown children live separately.
She **never uses AI** and insists on signed plant readings for control changes.
She builds **collective evidence** for funded human overrides instead of assuming a new plant role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her lead wage before a paid local water-safety opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a funded override role if agreed and a real bill-covering local vacancy would help.
